steps.body: A line plot stacks a mark above each measurement's spot on a number line. Measure five pencils in eighths — 1/2, 3/4, 1/2, 5/8, 1/2 — and every time 1/2 comes up again, another mark stacks on top of the last one, right above the 1/2 tick.
Build a line plot by stacking one X for each measurement.

widget.successFeedback: Every measurement has one X, and repeated values stack above the same tick.
widget.partialFeedback: Compare each stack with the data list. One X represents one measurement.

predict.prompt: Can one tick on a line plot carry MORE than one X?

options.label: Yes — one X per data value

predict.reveal: Repeated measurements pile up — every matching pencil stacks another X above the same tick. The height of a stack IS that value's count.

explanationVariants: 3/4 appears exactly once in the list — just one mark stacks above it.

widget.prompt: Using the same five pencils (1/2, 3/4, 1/2, 5/8, 1/2), how many marks stack above the 3/4 tick?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 counts every pencil in the whole list. Only one pencil measured 3/4: one mark.
3 is how many measured 1/2, not 3/4. Only one pencil measured 3/4: one mark.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count how many times 3/4 appears in the list.

steps.body: The **total** number of data points is every mark on the whole plot added together — every measurement counted once, no matter which tick it landed on.

explanationVariants: Three marks at 1/2, one at 5/8, one at 3/4: 3+1+1=5 total measurements.
Adding every stack's height gives the total count.

widget.prompt: A line plot has 3 marks at 1/2, 1 mark at 5/8, and 1 mark at 3/4. How many measurements are on the plot in all?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is only the tallest stack (at 1/2). Add every stack together: 3+1+1=5.
15 multiplies the stacks instead of adding them. Total data points add: 3+1+1=5.

widget.prompt: Six leaf lengths were measured: 3/8, 3/8, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 7/8. Sort each measurement to its tick.

items.label: Leaf F: 1/2 in
items.feedback: A third leaf at the 1/2 tick.

widget.missFeedback: Match each leaf's measurement to its own tick mark.
widget.successFeedback: Two leaves at 3/8, three at 1/2, one at 7/8 — the plot's three stacks.

explanationVariants: The 1/2 tick has 3 leaves stacked — more than any other tick (2 at 3/8, 1 at 7/8).

widget.prompt: For the six leaves (2 at 3/8, 3 at 1/2, 1 at 7/8), which tick has the TALLEST stack?

options.label: 1/2 — 3 leaves, more than any other tick
options.feedback: 3 leaves at 1/2 beats 2 at 3/8 and 1 at 7/8 — the tallest stack.

options.label: 3/8 — it was measured first
options.feedback: Measuring order doesn't matter — stack height does. 3/8 has only 2 leaves, fewer than 1/2's 3.

options.label: 7/8 — it's the biggest measurement
options.feedback: A bigger NUMBER doesn't mean a taller stack. 7/8 has only 1 leaf — the shortest stack here.

options.label: They're all the same height
options.feedback: They differ: 2, 3, and 1 leaves respectively. The 1/2 tick's stack of 3 is tallest.

hints: Count how many land on each tick.
Find which tick has the most.
explanationVariants: 3/8 has 2 seedlings, 1/2 has 3, and 7/8 has 1 — the 1/2 tick's stack of 3 is tallest.
Comparing the three stack heights, 1/2 wins with 3.

widget.prompt: Six seedlings measure: 3/8, 3/8, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, and 7/8 inch. How many seedlings are in the TALLEST stack on the line plot?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 counts every seedling in the whole dataset, not just one stack. The tallest single stack (at 1/2) has 3.
2 is the 3/8 stack's height, not the tallest. The 1/2 tick has 3 seedlings — the tallest stack.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count how many seedlings share each measurement, then find the biggest count.

steps.body: Data, stacked above a number line.
takeaways: A line plot stacks a mark above each measurement's tick — repeats stack higher.
The total data count adds up every stack's height.
The tallest stack shows the most common measurement, no matter its size.
steps.teaser: next: answering real questions using a finished line plot.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Count how many measurements share each value.** For 1/4, 1/4, 1/2: two measurements land on 1/4 (2 marks stack there), and one lands on 1/2 (1 mark).

widget.prompt: Three measurements are 1/4, 1/4, and 1/2. How many marks stack above the 1/4 tick?

options.feedback: 1/4 appears twice — two marks stack there.
3 counts every measurement in the list. Only two of them are 1/4.
